# Engine API reference

Engine **1.41.0** (host API 1.41), the latest release. Generated from the release's `starhermit.d.ts`; `starhermit types` writes the same file into your game.

This is the complete host API of the StarHermit engine for script games: every module a game imports
by name, every member, unit, limit and error. It follows the latest release only; a game pinned to an
older release has that release's `.starhermit/starhermit.d.ts` (from `starhermit types`) as its own
reference. New in host API 1.40 is summarised in [engine features](../engine-features.md); for a
guided start see the [engine tutorial](../tutorials/starhermit-engine.md) and the
[Football walkthrough](../tutorials/football.md). This reference is in English only.

| Module | Summary |
|---|---|
| [`starhermit:engine`](engine.md) | Lifecycle (`onStart`, `onFixedUpdate`, `onUpdate`, `onRender`), frames and timing, graphics levels, fuel and busy states, files, the game's manifest and runtime information. |
| [`starhermit:input`](input.md) | Actions bound from `control.*` lines, keyboard, pointer, touch and gamepads, rebinding and the on-screen controls. |
| [`starhermit:storage`](storage.md) | The game's private stores: key-value storage, `localStorage`, settings and cloud saves. |
| [`starhermit:scene`](scene.md) | The 3D scene after three.js r185: cameras, lights, meshes, geometries, materials, textures, loaders, animation, LOD, particles and the renderer. |
| [`starhermit:volume`](volume.md) | Volumetric effects: smoke, explosions, fire, dust, clouds and fog banks from presets, grids and `.wvdb` files (an engine extension). |
| [`starhermit:sky`](sky.md) | A physically based sky (`SkyAtmosphere`) with sun, moon, stars and aerial perspective, and three.js's Preetham `Sky` (host API 1.40). |
| [`starhermit:weather`](weather.md) | Wind (`WindField`), foliage sway, and weather visuals: clouds, rain, wet surfaces and lightning (host API 1.40). |
| [`starhermit:canvas`](canvas.md) | Off-screen 2D canvases after the web's CanvasRenderingContext2D, for textures and HUD images. |
| [`starhermit:draw`](draw.md) | The per-frame 2D overlay over the 3D scene (HUDs): shapes, images and text drawn in call order. |
| [`starhermit:ui`](ui.md) | The engine's immediate-mode UI for the game's own menus and HUD panels: widgets called every frame, layout, styles and focus. |
| [`starhermit:audio`](audio.md) | Sounds, music and the mixer after the Web Audio API. |
| [`starhermit:platform`](platform.md) | The StarHermit platform: the signed-in player, rooms and sockets, leaderboards, achievements, replays, chat and voice. |
| [`starhermit:world`](world.md) | Native per-entity work: tables, kernels and bindings that move thousands of objects without per-object script. |
| [`starhermit:physics`](physics.md) | 3D rigid bodies, colliders, joints, queries and a character controller, deterministic on every runtime (host API 1.40). |
| [`starhermit:script`](script.md) | Other realms: classic scripts, workers, the platform's sandboxed server script run locally, and authorities for client-side prediction. |
| [`starhermit:particles`](particles.md) | GPU particles (`GPUParticleEmitter`) and Solstice `.particles` effects (host API 1.40). |
| [`starhermit:vehicle`](vehicle.md) | Vehicle dynamics, tracks, lap timing and autopilots (host API 1.40). |
| [`starhermit:water`](water.md) | FFT oceans, ponds and water shading, with a deterministic wave field for gameplay (host API 1.40). |
| [`starhermit:surfaces`](surfaces.md) | Procedural tiling surfaces, terrain blending and grass (host API 1.40). |
| [Globals](globals.md) | `console`, timers and the other built-ins available without an import. |

## Conventions for every module

StarHermit host API, version 1: the built-in modules a script game imports by name (`import { onUpdate } from "starhermit:engine"`). The runtime (`starhermit`) is the only trusted code; a game package is data, and every host object it receives is an opaque handle the runtime validates on each call.

A game runs natively in the runtime's own interpreter and in browsers in the browser's engine (V8). What differs between the two (modules that import each other, built-ins only browsers have, local time, limits) is listed in spec/script-games.html, "Known differences between the native interpreter and V8"; `starhermit check` links the game's modules as browsers get them and warns of globals only browsers have.

Conventions for every module:

- Errors. A wrong argument type, a non-finite number where a number is needed, or a handle that was disposed, forged or belongs to another object throws a `TypeError`. Going past a limit (the manifest's `engine.limits.*`, a per-frame bound, a size) throws a `RangeError`. Where a web API is the model, its DOMException cases throw an `Error` whose `name` is the DOMException name (`IndexSizeError`, `SyntaxError`, `InvalidStateError`, `NotSupportedError`, `InvalidAccessError`, `NotAllowedError`), so `e.name` checks port unchanged. Platform calls reject with a `PlatformError` (`starhermit:platform`). Once the runtime has asked the game to stop, every host call throws.
- Units. World distances are meters, angles radians (except `PerspectiveCamera.fov`, degrees as in three.js), times seconds (platform timestamps are milliseconds since the Unix epoch, as the platform sends them), window coordinates physical pixels from the top-left corner (`frame().scale` converts to logical pixels).
- Colors (`ColorLike`) are sRGB: a CSS color string (`"#ff8800"`, `"rgb(255 136 0 / 50%)"`, a named color), a `0xRRGGBB` number, or `[r, g, b]` / `[r, g, b, a]` with components 0–1. Scene colors are converted to linear light for lighting, as three.js does.
- Light intensities. From API\_MINOR 23 they are three.js r155+'s (physically correct lights, its default since; r185's WebGLRenderer): a ported light keeps three.js's `intensity`. Direct light is `color × intensity × n·l` irradiance into three.js's BRDF (a Lambert material reflects `base / π` of it), and ambient and hemisphere light are irradiance through `BRDF_Lambert` of the diffuse color, `base × (1 − metalness) / π` (none on a metal). Before API\_MINOR 23 they keep the engine's legacy convention: a white surface facing a light of color 1 and intensity 1 shows its base color, three.js's legacy (pre-r155) scaling of ambient, hemisphere, directional, point and spot lights by π, ambient and hemisphere light on the whole base color; a light ported from r155+ there uses `threeIntensity / Math.PI`. At every minor point and spot lights fall off as r155+'s do (the inverse `decay` power of the distance, with its windowed `distance`), so a legacy port's falloff does not carry over, and emissive light and `scene.environment` are three.js r155+'s (no factor); there are no RectAreaLights.
- Callbacks. Lifecycle callbacks are registered once at the top level of the entry module; input events arrive at the start of each frame, before `onFixedUpdate`. Asynchronous host work (asset loads, platform calls, permission prompts) resolves promises between frames; waiting on it costs no fuel and never counts as not responding.
- Resources. A handle's resource (a node, mesh, material, texture, canvas, bitmap, sound, socket, worker…) counts against its budget until `dispose()`, `close()` or `release()`, which free it at once, or until the collector finds the handle unreachable: natively at the end of the call in which that collection ends, which the runtime drives as the game makes scene and canvas resources, so dropped ones are released before their budgets fill; and a creation a budget would refuse first collects and releases what was dropped. In browsers the browser's collector decides when, so dispose what you drop when a budget is tight.
- Version. `engine.API_VERSION` is this file's major version (the manifest's `engine.api=1`); minor versions only add members.

Tools. The runtime carries this file and the developer commands, so a game needs nothing else: `starhermit new DIR` writes a new script game pinned to the runtime's engine release, `starhermit types DIR` writes this file as `DIR/.starhermit/starhermit.d.ts` (a dot-name, so no package carries it; the game's tsconfig.json lists it), `starhermit check DIR` validates the package and plays it headless, `starhermit DIR` plays it, `starhermit package --native DIR` writes its file index for a folder upload the StarHermit client installs and plays natively, and `starhermit package --web DIR --out UPLOAD` writes its web upload, its loader pinned to the same release on https://wiki.starhermit.com/engine/. `cargo starhermit` has the same commands for engine developers.

Modules. Scripts are ECMAScript modules; `import` takes the built-in `starhermit:<module>` names and package files by a specifier relative to the importing file (`"./logic/pose.ts"`, `"../shared/sim.js"`); there are no bare specifiers, package-absolute paths or import maps. A specifier that names an existing package file loads it. Otherwise one ending in `.js` or `.mjs` loads the `.ts` or `.mts` file of the same stem (the TypeScript compiler's convention), and an extensionless one tries `.ts`, `.mts`, `.js` and `.mjs` in that order; directories are not resolved to an index file. A query string or fragment on a relative specifier (`"./settings.js?v=11"`, web cache-busting) is ignored for resolution: a module's identity is its resolved path, so `./a.js?v=1` and `./a.js` are one module, evaluated once. A specifier that resolves to nothing, or outside the package, ends the game on the error screen naming the importing file and the specifier. Dynamic `import()` resolves the same way and rejects instead. `"moduleResolution": "bundler"` with `"allowImportingTsExtensions": true` type-checks every accepted form.

Language. Strict-mode ECMAScript 2022 plus TypeScript syntax (erased). Natively the interpreter erases the types; on the web the same eraser hands each module to the browser's engine as JavaScript with every line where it was (columns too, but on the line of an enum or of a parameter property's constructor or class body), and `starhermit check` parses and links what it hands over. Supported: annotations and return types anywhere (also over several lines before an arrow's `=>`), generics (`<T,>(x: T) => x` in arrows), `as`, `as const`, `satisfies`, `!`, `x!: T`, optional members, `declare` fields and declarations, `abstract` classes and members, overloads, index signatures, interfaces and type aliases, `import type`, `export type` and inline `type` specifiers (an import used only as a type is left out), `implements`, accessibility and `readonly` modifiers, enums and const enums (compiled to objects) and parameter properties (fields declared before the class's own and assigned as the constructor starts, after `super()`: TypeScript for ES2022). Not supported, refused natively and by check: decorators, value namespaces (type-only namespaces erase), `import x = require()` and `import x = N.y`, auto-accessors, JSX, `<T>x` assertions broken across lines after `return`, `throw` or `yield` (use `as`), and line breaks in an async arrow's type parameters (`async <T>` and its `(` on different lines); none of these would be JavaScript once erased. BigInt is included (literals, operators, `BigInt.asIntN`/`asUintN`, `BigInt64Array`, `BigUint64Array`, DataView's BigInt accessors, exact `toLocaleString` and `Intl.NumberFormat`). A BigInt holds at most 1,048,576 bits (2^20, about 315,000 decimal digits; V8 allows more): a result past that is a `RangeError` ("Maximum BigInt size exceeded"), and large-number work counts against the script's fuel like any other. The host API takes no BigInt: numeric and data parameters throw a `TypeError` for one (convert with `Number(x)` or `String(x)` first), `JSON.stringify` (so storage, saves, workers and platform calls) throws, `BigInt64Array`/`BigUint64Array` are not accepted where a typed array of numbers is, and `starhermit:world` kernels refuse BigInt (their numbers are doubles). Scene property fields convert one as `Number(x)` does, as the browser's engine does. `console.log(12n)` prints `12n`. Of `Intl` and the locale-aware members, these follow the player's language (BCP 47 tags; others fall back to it): `String.prototype. localeCompare` and `Intl.Collator` (Unicode root collation with `sensitivity` and `numeric`), `String.prototype.normalize`, `Number.prototype.toLocaleString` and `Intl.NumberFormat` (`style` decimal, percent, currency and unit; `currency` with `currencyDisplay` symbol, narrowSymbol, code or name and `currencySign` standard or accounting, digits defaulting to the currency's (JPY 0, KWD 3); fraction and integer digit options, `useGrouping`; `format`, `formatToParts`), `Date.prototype.toLocaleDateString`/`TimeString`/ `String` and `Intl.DateTimeFormat` (`dateStyle`, `timeStyle`, the numeric and short/long field options, `timeZone` "UTC" or the system's), `Intl.PluralRules` (`select`) and `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat`. Other `Intl` members are absent.

The project's tsconfig should use `"lib": ["ES2022"]` (which declares BigInt and the BigInt typed arrays) and `"types": []`: the runtime is not a browser and has no DOM. The [globals](globals.md) are the only ones beyond ECMAScript.
